lead: Speech reaches the brain through a mechanical spectrum analyser. The ear splits sound into overlapping frequency bands, and a different set of hair cells serves each band. Two tones in the same band interfere; two tones in different bands do not. This is why speech systems space their filters by perception and not by hertz. The mel and Bark scales put that spacing into a formula, and mel-spaced filter banks are the front end that produces MFCCs, the standard feature vector for speech recognition.
prereq: You need 7.3 for the magnitude spectrum of a frame and 7.2 for where speech energy sits.

sections.h3: The ear as a bank of filters

blocks.text: Sound first meets the outer ear: the pinna and a canal about 2.5 cm long. The canal behaves like a tube closed at one end and resonates near 3 kHz, adding a few decibels in the 2–5 kHz range. That is exactly where the weak consonants of speech carry much of their information.

The middle ear, behind the eardrum, is three small bones: malleus, incus and stapes. They match the low acoustic impedance of air to the much higher impedance of the fluid in the inner ear. Without that matching, most of the sound would reflect off the fluid surface. A small muscle reflex stiffens the chain for very loud sounds.

The inner ear holds the cochlea, a coiled, fluid-filled tube. Along its length runs the basilar membrane, narrow and stiff at the base and wide and slack at the apex. A pure tone makes the membrane vibrate most strongly at one place: high frequencies near the base, low frequencies near the apex. Hair cells at that place bend and fire the auditory nerve.

This is the place theory of pitch: the brain reads frequency mainly from which place is active, with firing rate helping at low frequencies. The practical point for us: each place answers a band of frequencies, and neighbouring places answer overlapping bands. The ear is a bank of filters, not one Fourier transform of the whole signal.

sections.h3: Critical bands and the Bark scale

blocks.text: Play a tone together with a narrow band of noise. As the noise bandwidth grows, the tone becomes harder to hear, but only up to a limit. Past that bandwidth, extra noise changes nothing. That limit is the critical band around the tone's frequency.

So a critical band is the range of frequencies within which a second sound interferes with the first. Two components inside one critical band mask each other; two components in different bands are heard separately.

About 24 critical bands cover 20 Hz to 16 kHz. The width is nearly constant at roughly 100 Hz between 100 Hz and 500 Hz, then grows with the centre frequency, reaching a few kilohertz at the top. The Bark scale numbers these bands: one Bark is one critical band, so the scale runs from 0 to about 24. Below 500 Hz, z ≈ f/100, with f in hertz and z in Bark, so 300 Hz sits at about z = 3 Bark, at the edge between the third and fourth critical band.

Some syllabi call the critical band the Bark band. Filter banks in coders and recognisers place one filter per band, so a wide high-frequency band gets one filter where a linear scale would give twenty.

blocks.where: f is frequency in hertz; mel is the perceived pitch in mel. The constants are chosen so that 1000 Hz maps to exactly 1000 mel, which anchors the scale.

blocks.text: Below about 700 Hz the curve is still steep: near 0 Hz its slope is roughly 1.6 mel per hertz, and 100 Hz is about 150 mel. Averaged over 0 to 1000 Hz the slope is 1 mel per hertz, because 1000 Hz is the anchor at 1000 mel. Above 1 kHz the curve flattens into a logarithm. Each doubling of frequency then adds about 500 to 780 mel, approaching 781 mel (2595 × log₁₀ 2) at high frequencies. 1000 Hz is 1000 mel, 2000 Hz is about 1521 mel, and 4000 Hz is about 2146 mel. The figure plots the curve against a line that treats hertz directly as mel.

Why this suits speech: the first formant of most vowels lies below 1 kHz and the second below about 3 kHz, while energy above 4 kHz is weak. A linear filter bank would spend half its filters on the empty top of the range and would merge two neighbouring formants below 1 kHz into one band. Mel spacing gives more bands where the energy is concentrated.

Masking is the reason bands matter. A loud low tone hides a quiet higher tone far more than the reverse; this is the upward spread of masking. Masking also works in time: forward masking lasts up to about 100–200 ms after the masker, backward masking a few milliseconds before it.

The just-noticeable difference (JND) is the smallest frequency change a listener can detect. Near 100 Hz it is a few hertz; near 10 kHz it is a few tens of hertz. In relative terms it is roughly 0.3 % over most of the range, which is another reason a perceptual scale must be logarithmic at high frequencies.

Loudness has its own scales. The loudness level in phon of a sound is the sound pressure level in decibels of a 1 kHz tone that sounds equally loud. The sone is a ratio scale: 1 sone is defined at 40 phon, and each rise of 10 phon doubles the sone value. Equal-loudness contours, measured by Fletcher and Munson and standardised later, show that the ear is most sensitive around 2–5 kHz, where the ear canal resonates.

examples.question: Using mel(f) = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f/700), convert 300 Hz, 1000 Hz and 8000 Hz to mel. Then find what percentage of the mel range from 0 Hz to 8000 Hz is used by the first 1000 Hz.
steps: Fix the units: f is in hertz and the answer is in mel.
For f = 1000 Hz: 1 + 1000/700 = 2.4286, and log₁₀(2.4286) = 0.3854. mel = 2595 × 0.3854 = 1000, which is the anchor of the scale.
examples.answer: 300 Hz = 402 mel, 1000 Hz = 1000 mel, 8000 Hz = 2840 mel, and the first 1000 Hz takes 35.2 % of the mel range up to 8000 Hz.

traps: Mel is perceptual, not physical. Do not subtract two mel values and call the result hertz; convert back with f = 700 × (10^(mel/2595) − 1).
Mixing units in a filter-bank question: a filter centre given in mel compared with a bandwidth given in hertz. Convert both to one unit first.
Critical bands are equal in width on the Bark scale, not in hertz. One band near 300 Hz is about 100 Hz wide; one band near 6 kHz is about a kilohertz wide.
The mel formula uses log base 10. If you switch to the natural log, the constant must change from 2595 to 1127; keeping 2595 with ln inflates the answer by a factor of about 2.3.
1000 Hz is not the top of the mel scale. It is the anchor point; 8000 Hz is about 2840 mel and higher frequencies go further.

quiz.q: State the place theory of pitch.
quiz.a: Pitch is read from the position along the basilar membrane where vibration is strongest. High frequencies peak near the stiff base, low frequencies near the slack apex. Firing rate also carries pitch at low frequencies.

quiz.q: Write the mel formula and state the point that fixes its constants.
quiz.a: mel = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f/700), with f in hertz. The constants are fixed so that 1000 Hz maps to exactly 1000 mel.

quiz.q: Why does the middle ear exist, and what would happen without it?
quiz.a: It matches the low impedance of air to the high impedance of cochlear fluid, using the area ratio of eardrum to oval window and the lever action of the three bones. Without it most sound energy would reflect at the fluid surface and hearing would be far less sensitive.

quiz.q: Convert 700 Hz and 4000 Hz to mel using mel = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f/700).
A 300 Hz tone strongly masks a 350 Hz tone, but a 300 Hz tone barely masks a 3000 Hz tone. Explain using critical bands.
quiz.a: The critical band near 300 Hz is about 100 Hz wide, so 300 Hz and 350 Hz fall inside one band and compete for the same hair cells. 3000 Hz lies many bands away, so its hair cells are unaffected. Masking also spreads upward more than downward, which is why the low tone hides the higher one more easily than the reverse.

quiz.q: Distinguish the phon and the sone.
quiz.a: The phon is loudness level: it equals the sound pressure level in decibels of a 1 kHz tone that sounds equally loud. The sone is a ratio scale of loudness: 1 sone is defined at 40 phon, and each 10 phon increase doubles the sone value.

quiz.q: Using z ≈ f/100 below 500 Hz, give the Bark number of 300 Hz. Compare it with the mel value of 402 and say what the comparison shows.
quiz.a: z ≈ 300/100 = 3 Bark. This means 300 Hz is about three critical-band widths above 0 Hz. Both Bark and mel are continuous perceptual scales; they differ in what they compress — Bark follows critical-band width, mel follows judged pitch — so the two numbers are not interchangeable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many modern front ends replace triangular mel filters with gammatone filters, whose impulse response is a tone under a gamma-shaped envelope, and the matching perceptual scale is the ERB scale of Glasberg and Moore. Audio codecs such as MP3 and Opus carry a psychoacoustic model that computes masking thresholds per critical band and drops the bits the ear will not miss. Cochlear implants use place coding directly, stimulating electrodes at different positions along the basilar membrane. Useful search terms: gammatone filterbank, ERB scale, psychoacoustic model.
